Product: Digital Tracker (launched 2021) and TV Tracker (2023), one Media Tracking team since 2024 My part: Digital Journey: brand, onboarding, the browser extension and the mobile Safari extension Panel: Verified HCPs and patients, opted in; informed consent, no personal data captured Scale: 400,000+ ad impressions captured a month, insights every two weeks (ZoomRx)

The problem: Most pharma media measurement is modelled: household TV ratings, or digital exposure inferred from pixels, arriving months late. ZoomRx observes instead. Verified physicians and patients install an extension that passively records the healthcare ads, sites, emails and AI answers they see, and the same people are later surveyed on what they recalled. That turns on one thing: a doctor agreeing to install a tracker. The panelist experience had to make consent clear, privacy believable and the reward obvious. How do you get a busy physician to install a browser tracker, keep it switched on for months, and feel in control the whole time? Consent is the product: The data is only as good as the opt-in; every screen says what is captured and what is not. Value per permission: People agree more readily when each permission has its own visible reward and can be switched off on its own. Out of sight, out of mind: An extension runs silently; its pop-up has to show at a glance that today is counting, or panelists drift away.

Goals: Plain-language consent: Modules a panelist can read, tick and untick. Fast, safe set-up: From invite to active extension in a few steps, on desktop and on a phone. Stay switched on: An extension that reassures, nudges and helps without nagging.

Key decisions: Modules, each with its value: Healthcare web browsing, exposure to healthcare ads and promotional emails are separate modules, each with its own monthly value and checkbox, adding up to a total monthly earning potential above a single Start Earning button. Privacy said first, in plain words: Before any choice: non-healthcare content and anything from web-based CRMs or EHRs is never retained, and only what the panelist opted to share is captured. An invite code, not a password: Sign-in is a six-box invite code with the terms to accept, and a link to use existing ZoomRx credentials for panelists who already have them. The extension as a status light: Its pop-up opens on whether today counts (Active Today) and when the panelist was last compensated, then one line per module saying what is monitored on this site, with their consent. Nudge, don’t nag: A switched-off module shows a grey state and one sentence suggesting it be turned back on, never a blocking alert. Email by forwarding: Promotional emails are captured by a Forward Email action, so the extension never reads an inbox. One brand across the touchpoints: A compass-star mark built around the ZoomRx Z, a classic serif for greetings and a clean sans for the interface, electric blue for actions and teal for anything to do with earnings.

What Media Tracking captures (ZoomRx): Paid search: The queries physicians run, competitor ad copy, trigger keywords and landing pages. Banners and email: Endemic and non-endemic display, static and video; manufacturer, rep and third-party email. Healthcare browsing: Sites visited, content read and time on site. Med AI: Answers from Google AI Overviews, ChatGPT and other medical AI tools. TV, linear and streaming: Exposure identified by audio fingerprinting across broadcast, cable and streaming. Recall and lift: Phase two surveys the same panelists on ad recall, brand lift and intent to act. Outcome: Digital Journey is how panelists join and stay in the Digital Tracker. ZoomRx reports 400,000+ ad impressions captured a month from 100% verified HCP and patient panels, insights every two weeks against the 8 to 12 week lag of TV ratings, and the industry’s first coverage of medical AI answers. Those are the product’s figures, not measured results of my design.
Honest limits: Panel sizes, client names and commercial terms stay internal. The amounts on the module screens are the design’s, shown as delivered; a colleague’s name is blurred.

Safura (AI Assistant). Safura, which began as PAIA (Personal Artificial Intelligence App), is a personal AI assistant for Android that answers the calls you would rather not take. A warm AI voice picks up unknown and declined calls in Hindi or English; you can read the call live as text, steer it or take it back, and every call ends in a short summary of what was asked, what Safura did and what you need to do. I designed the product end to end: the brand, the app and its landing page. Product: A personal AI call assistant for Android Calls it takes: Unknown numbers and calls you decline; contacts and emergency calls always ring you Languages: Hindi and English, with a male or female voice Privacy: A text transcript only, never audio; kept 7 days, 30 days, 1 year or not at all

The problem: Unknown numbers are a daily tax in India: delivery riders lost on the way, insurance renewals, property and credit-card pitches, and telemarketers, mixed in with calls that matter. Ignoring them means missing the important ones; answering them all wastes the day. An assistant can sit in between, but only if people trust it with their phone. How do you hand your phone calls to an AI and still feel completely in control of them? Never between you and your people: Trust starts with what the assistant will not touch: saved contacts and emergency calls. Watching beats trusting blind: Seeing the conversation as it happens, with a way to intervene, is what lets people let go. A summary, not a recording: People want the outcome and the next step, not to listen back to audio. Goals: Take the right calls: Unknown and declined calls only, each route switchable. Keep you in the loop: Live transcript, steering and take-over at any moment. Tell you only what matters: A three-part summary and a clear tag on every call.

Key decisions: Two routes, both switchable: Saved contacts and emergency numbers ring you as always; unknown numbers and calls you decline go to Safura. “Answer unknown calls” and “Answer declined calls” are separate switches in Settings. Live, with a steering wheel: During a call the transcript appears as it is said, with quick suggestions (take a message, ask them to call back later, say I’m busy), a box for your own note, and Take the call or End call. Safura works the note into what it says next instead of reading it out. Every summary in three questions: What the caller asked, what Safura did, and what is needed from you, with the answer coloured: an urgent action in red, spam in amber, nothing needed in green. Call back, report as spam and the full transcript sit underneath. Tags that sort the day: URGENT, SPAM and FYI on every call in the list, grouped by day, under a week view of calls handled, time saved and calls missed. Brief it once: Voice, greeting language (Auto, Hindi or English), delivery instructions, availability, and the kinds of calls it may handle for you: property, credit card, delivery, insurance. Privacy as a feature: No audio, ever; transcripts with a retention you choose; Pause Safura without losing your set-up; delete the account and everything goes. The promises are repeated on onboarding, not hidden in a policy. Set up in four steps: Verify your number, give three permissions on one screen, set up the assistant, then run a test call to hear how Safura greets your callers.

What Safura does: Answers for you: Unknown and declined calls, in Hindi or English. Live transcript: Read the call as it happens; steer it or take over. Call summaries: Asked, did, needed from you, with call back and transcript. Spam handled quietly: Telemarketers ended politely and reportable for the community. Weekly view: Calls handled, spam blocked, time saved and calls missed. Works with your phone: Your own dialler and number, through call forwarding Safura sets up. Outcome: Safura is designed end to end for Android: brand, onboarding, the live call, summaries, settings and a landing page that explains it in the same voice. It is free to start, and Android only for now. Honest limits: An early product; no usage numbers are claimed. Names and numbers in the screens are sample data.

Naxxum Optima (Procure to Pay). Optima P2P is Naxxum’s cloud procure-to-pay application, listed on the Microsoft Marketplace: one place for a company to run buying from the first purchase request through proposals, orders, delivery receipts and invoices to payment, with its suppliers, catalogue and reporting alongside. I designed the web portal: the brand, sign-up and the working screens procurement teams use every day. Client: Naxxum, an IT services group with offices in Paris (Puteaux) and Doha Product: Optima P2P, a procure-to-pay SaaS on the Microsoft Marketplace Users: Procurement, finance and the suppliers they buy from Scope: Brand and log-in, the portal’s navigation, configuration and supplier management

The problem: Buying in a mid-sized company runs through emails, spreadsheets and an ERP that only finance can use: a request becomes a quote, an order, a delivery and an invoice, and each step lives somewhere else. Optima brings the whole procure-to-pay chain into one cloud application that automates the manual steps, enforces the company’s controls and still connects to the ERP it already runs. How do you make a procurement system that holds every rule a finance team needs, yet stays simple enough for anyone who has to buy something? The chain is the navigation: Requests, proposals, orders, invoices and receipts are steps in one flow, so the menu follows that order. Set up once, used daily: Companies, locations, taxes and suppliers are configured rarely but shape every transaction, so configuration needs to be thorough but calm. Tables are the work: Most of the day is spent in lists: they need status at a glance, sorting, paging and actions on each row.

Goals: One flow, end to end: Every procure-to-pay step reachable from one sidebar. Calm configuration: Long set-up broken into tabs and short dialogs. Fast, legible lists: Consistent tables with status, sorting and row actions.

Key decisions: A sidebar in the order of the work: My dashboard, then purchase requests, requests for proposal, purchase orders, invoices and receipts of delivery, followed by categories, articles, suppliers, reporting and configuration. Tabs for big records: A company is general information, locations, departments, users, taxes, processes and customisation; a supplier is general information, users, documents and alerts. One tab at a time, Save & Continue at the top. Dialogs for small additions: A new location or an edited document opens over the list, so the context never disappears. Status you can read across the room: Active and inactive as solid blue and red pills, the same in every table. One table pattern everywhere: Sortable headers, row action menus, an item count and pagination with a page-size control, so every list works the same way. A brand for a new product: An N mark cut from a blue square, a two-line wordmark, and a log-in and sign-up with an illustrated brand panel; sign-up is split into two steps with a live password-strength meter.

What Optima covers: Purchase requests: Raise a need and route it for approval. Requests for proposal: Ask suppliers to quote and compare. Purchase orders: Turn an approved request into an order. Invoices and receipts: Match what was ordered, delivered and billed. Suppliers: Payment conditions, contacts, documents with expiry and alerts. Configuration and reporting: Companies, locations, departments, taxes and processes; real-time reporting. Outcome: Optima P2P is published by Naxxum on the Microsoft Marketplace as a SaaS procure-to-pay application, with automation, real-time visibility, vendor management and ERP integration. Honest limits: Freelance design work; usage figures stay with the client. Names in the screens are sample data, and the client’s own name and photo are blurred.

Kosh Crypto (Crypto Investing). Kosh was a Mumbai crypto start-up with one idea: instead of betting on a single coin, invest in a bucket. Each bucket is a curated basket of crypto assets built around a theme, so when one coin falls others can hold it up, and the swings land closer to the middle than any single coin’s. I led the design of the app, from the brand illustration to investing, the portfolio and the wallet, in light and dark. Client: Kosh Crypto, Mumbai, founded 2021 Product: Investing in expertly curated buckets of crypto assets Users: New and experienced investors in India, investing in rupees Themes: Light and dark, switchable from the profile The problem: Crypto drew a wave of first-time investors in India, and they faced the same two problems: which coin to pick, out of thousands, and how to live with prices that can halve in a week. Picking one coin concentrates the risk. Kosh’s answer was the bucket: a ready-made, diversified basket around an idea, like a hedge against the rupee, that spreads the bet so that losses and gains average out.

How do you make crypto feel like a considered investment rather than a bet, for someone who has never bought a coin? Pick an idea, not a coin: Beginners understand a goal, like beating inflation, faster than a ticker. Show the spread: Seeing the money split across buckets is what makes diversification real. Habit beats timing: Small amounts on a schedule are easier to start, and less exposed to one bad day, than a single big buy. Goals: Invest in a theme: Buckets with a plain-language reason to exist. Start small and steady: A recurring plan as the default, one-time as the option. Always know where you stand: Portfolio, performance and wallet a tap apart.

Key decisions: Buckets named for what they do: “Hedge against INR”: concerned about currency inflation? This bucket is designed to beat it. Each bucket card leads with the idea and its recent change, then one Invest Now button; trending buckets scroll sideways on home. The portfolio as a donut: Home opens on the total value and the gain since the start, inside a ring split by bucket with each share in per cent, and the portfolio’s age below: the diversification is the picture. A recurring plan by default: Investing opens on AIP, an automatic investment plan, with daily, weekly or monthly; One Time is the second tab. A minimum is stated up front and the wallet balance sits beside the amount. Amounts in one tap: A large, editable rupee figure with +1000, +2000, +2500 and +3000 chips to build it quickly. Swipe up to confirm: Money moves only on a deliberate swipe, not an easily mis-tapped button. Performance, then the reasoning: A bucket page shows its change and a line chart with 1h to All time ranges, then Overview and Weightage: why the bucket exists and what is in it. Rupees in, rupees out, verified: The profile opens on the INR wallet with Deposit and Withdraw INR, the KYC-verified badge, banks, history, help and a theme switch.

What the app does: Curated buckets: Thematic baskets of crypto assets, with performance and weightage. Recurring or one time: AIP daily, weekly or monthly, or a single investment. Portfolio view: Total value, gain and the split across buckets. INR wallet: Deposit, withdraw, manage banks and transaction history. KYC: Verified identity before investing. Light and dark: Two complete themes from one design system. Outcome: The designs cover the whole investing loop, from choosing a bucket to a recurring plan, the portfolio and the rupee wallet, in two complete themes. Honest limits: The company was a small early-stage start-up and few public details remain; amounts and names in the screens are sample data, and nothing here describes investment returns.

TaxVolt (Tax Filing). TaxVolt is a tax filing app and website for Canadians: estimate your refund for free, then prepare and e-file your return on your phone, slip by slip, with the refund updating as you go. Its line sums up the promise: it is not what you make, it is what you keep. I designed the product, from the crowned-lion brand to the filing flow, for Zazz, the agency that built it. Product: Tax estimation and e-filing for individuals, the self-employed and small businesses Market: Canada: CRA forms, T4 slips, provincial tax and HST Built by: Zazz, design to launch in four months Platforms: Android app and a website with pricing by filer type The problem: Filing taxes is stressful for most people: unfamiliar forms, credits nobody explains, and the fear of a mistake. Paid tools are built around the form, not the person filling it in. TaxVolt set out to make filing feel guided and even rewarding, with a refund you can watch grow and a free estimate before anyone pays.

How do you walk someone through a tax return, slip by slip, without ever making them feel they are filling in a government form? Start with the money: People engage when they can see what they will get back, so the refund leads every screen. Let them try first: A free estimate lowers the stakes before sign-up and payment. One question at a time: Personal questions as single toggles beat a long form full of boxes. Goals: Guided filing: Clear steps from personal details to results. Fewer mistakes: Plain questions, explanations at hand, automatic checks. Trust: A strong, confident brand around sensitive financial data.

Key decisions: The refund on top, always: A live estimated refund heads the return and changes as answers go in; the end screen celebrates it with confetti and a three-line summary of withholdings, liability and refund. Four tabs for the whole return: Personal, Income, Deductions and Results: the return reads as four short chapters instead of one long form. Questions as toggles: Are you married? Can someone claim you as a dependant? Each question stands alone with a switch and an info icon for the why. Slips by their real names: Income is entered slip by slip, T4, T5007, T4E, T4A, each with its full CRA name, a Begin button and Learn more, so people match the paper in their hand. A free estimator at the front door: Home offers the refund estimator next to Sign in, with a comparison of the year’s new tax credits, so the first experience is a free answer. A crest with a promise: A crowned lion in green, white and yellow, and the line “It is not what you make, it is what you keep. Let us help!” on the splash. Pricing by who you are: The website sorts plans by filer type, such as full- or part-time employees and the self-employed with rental income, each with its price.

What TaxVolt does: Refund estimator: A free estimate before signing in, with new-credit comparison. Guided return: Personal, income, deductions and results, with the refund live. Income slips: Every CRA slip type, entered one at a time. Credits: All federal and provincial credits and taxes listed with their amounts. E-file: Prepare and file the year’s return in the app. Share: Invite friends from the results screen. Outcome: TaxVolt launched on Android with the website. Zazz, the agency that built it, reports 100,000+ downloads in the first six months, 40% better user retention and 30% faster tax filing; those are the agency’s figures for the product, not measured results of my design. Honest limits: Agency work; the figures are Zazz’s and come without baselines. The onboarding copy in the screens is placeholder text from the design stage.

Voohoo Live (Live Streaming). Voohoo Live is a live-streaming and short-video app by AdCounty: creators go live, post photos and videos, and earn from virtual gifts that fans send, which turn into diamonds they can spend or redeem. I led the redesign of the app and its website: the brand, live streams and battles, the feed, leaderboards, games and the creator profile. Client: AdCounty (AdCounty Apps / AdCounty Media) Product: Live streams, short video and photos, with gifts, diamonds and games Platforms: Android, iOS and the web Category: Social and communication, free to use The problem: Live streaming is a crowded market, and the old app made people work to find a stream, follow a creator or send a gift. In a gift economy that friction is lost income for creators and for the platform. The brief was a redesign that made watching, gifting and competing effortless, with a look lively enough to stand out. How do you make a live-streaming app feel like a party, while keeping gifts, diamonds and battles simple enough that anyone joins in?

Status drives gifting: Fans give to be seen: the star gifter, the leaderboard, the badge on the profile. Competition draws a crowd: Battles between two creators, with a timer and a split screen, pull viewers in better than any feed. Live first, everything else second: The home screen should open on what is happening right now. Goals: Find a stream in seconds: Live on top, with clear filters and viewer counts. Make gifting rewarding: Visible recognition for gifters and earnings for creators. One look across app and web: A bold brand that carries from phone to browser.

Key decisions: Live, Photos, Rewards: The home opens on three tabs with Live first, a rotating banner for events like the star gifter of the month, and colour-coded filters: All, WOW Battle, Popular, Upcoming. Cards that sell the moment: Each live card shows the creator, a Follow button, a Live tag and how many are watching; battle cards split two creators with a VS badge and the time running. A stream built for taking part: In a stream: gifts and diamonds by the host’s name, the viewer count, a collab switch to bring guests in on side tiles, chat over the video, and a toolbar ending in the gift box. Leaderboards with a podium: Top Earners, Top Spenders and Top Events, with the top two on cards and a crown for number one, then the ranked list with gifts, diamonds and follow states. Profiles that show standing: Fans, following, posts and likes, coins spent and diamonds held, with badges and a frame around the photo. Games in the hub: A games section on web and app (car racing, cricket, cards and more) to keep the audience between streams. A brand that moves: A violet play-button mark with a handwritten “live”, on violet-to-lilac gradients, and a web log-in with phone, Facebook or Google plus store codes.

What Voohoo does: Live streams and collabs: Go live alone or with guests, with chat and a viewer count. WOW Battles: Creator against creator, live, on a timer. Gifts and diamonds: Fans send gifts; creators collect diamonds to spend or redeem. Photos and short video: A feed with likes, comments and shares. Leaderboards: Top earners, top spenders and top events. Games and V-Store: Games between streams and a store for in-app items. Outcome: The redesigned Voohoo Live shipped on Android, iOS and the web and is still updated, at version 2.44 in October 2025 on its Android listing. The redesign played a part in bringing more than 250,000 new users to the platform. Honest limits: Names and numbers in the screens are sample data; some secondary copy is placeholder text from the design stage.

ThatsGame (Sports Mentoring). ThatsGame is a basketball platform where young athletes rise: they upload their game, and professional players watch it and answer with personal critique, comments and guidance. Pros also share training insight as Pro Talks in audio and video. I designed the app and the website: the feed, the critique flow, uploads and the creator dashboard. Client: ThatsGame LLC Users: Young basketball players, and the pros who mentor them Platforms: iOS, Android and the web Content: Pro Talks, critique videos and community posts The problem: Talented young players rarely get in front of a professional. Coaching is expensive, scouts are few, and a highlight reel on social media gets likes, not feedback. ThatsGame offers a direct line: post a clip of your game and a pro tells you what to fix, while everyone else learns from the pros’ talks. How do you make a kid’s first upload feel worth a professional’s time, and make giving feedback quick enough that pros keep doing it?

Three kinds of content: Pros teaching, players asking for critique, and everyone else talking basketball need separate homes. Uploading must be easy: Young players film on a phone; trimming and posting can’t need an editing tool. Feedback should be fast: A pro’s reaction has to take seconds: tap a phrase, say a sentence. Goals: Learn from pros: Pro Talks first in the feed. Get critiqued: A clear path from a clip to a pro’s feedback. See your progress: Your uploads, views and reactions over time.

Key decisions: The feed in three tabs: ProTalks, Critique and Other: learning from pros, asking for feedback and the community each have their own lane, with a filter for the rest. Critique as a post type: Upload Video or Upload Audio, trim the clip on a filmstrip, then title, description, category and a thumbnail; Publish sends it for critique, Save to vault keeps it for later. Reactions in one tap: Comments offer ready phrases (Fantastic, Good job, Get back in the gym), a text box and a voice note, so a pro can respond in seconds. A dashboard for creators: Views, likes, dislikes, comments and watch time for recent posts, with a 24-hour graph and credits, followers and following beside them. The content vault: Everything recorded or picked from the gallery sits in a vault until it is ready to post. Bold, sporty, simple: A red TG monogram between spaced capitals, one basketball red for every action, and full-bleed game photos.

What ThatsGame does: Pro Talks: Audio and video training insight from professional players. Critique videos: Upload your game and get a pro’s feedback and comments. Community: Share clips, react and connect with players worldwide. Creator dashboard: Views, likes, comments and watch time over time. Content vault: Record, keep and publish when ready. Get discovered: Exposure to mentors, scouts and fans. Outcome: ThatsGame is live on the App Store, Google Play and the web, and still updated in 2026, with Pro Talks, critique and mentorship at its core as designed. Honest limits: Names and copy in the screens are placeholders from the design stage; no usage figures are claimed.

MyParkings (Smart Parking). MyParkings is a smart parking app and website for South Delhi, launched in October 2021 by Union Minister Anurag Thakur for the South Delhi Municipal Corporation: see which municipal lots have space, book a slot for a car or bike in advance, and check in and out with a QR code, cashless and paperless. I led the design of the app and the website. For: South Delhi Municipal Corporation, built and run by BECIL Network: 145 surface, 6 multi-level and 2 automated parking sites Users: Drivers and riders in South Delhi, and attendants at the lots Launch: 14 October 2021, by the Union Minister for Information and Broadcasting The problem: Finding parking in South Delhi means circling blocks, queueing at lots that turn out to be full, and paying cash for a paper slip. The corporation runs well over a hundred lots, but a driver had no way to know which had space. MyParkings put the whole network on a map with live availability, and replaced the slip with a booking and a QR code.

How do you make a city-wide parking system feel as simple as booking a cab, for every driver from a first-time smartphone user to a daily commuter? Distance on foot matters: People choose a lot by how far they must walk afterwards, not by the address. Availability is the answer: Slots left, shown before the tap, saves the wasted drive. The receipt is the ticket: At the gate, one scannable code beats any number or paper slip. Goals: Find a spot fast: Every lot on a map, filtered by vehicle. Book in seconds: Date, time and hours, price shown up front. Paperless at the gate: A QR receipt for check-in and check-out.

Key decisions: Map first, filtered by vehicle: The app opens on the map with Car and Bike filters; each lot is a pin, and the route and walking time to it are drawn as you choose. A card with everything to decide: The lot card shows its name and address, walking time and distance, slots left, price per hour and a favourite heart, above one Book Spot button. Time picked like a cab ride: Date, start time and number of hours on one sheet, with a scroll of days and plus or minus for hours; the summary reads “Today 1:30 PM to 4:30 PM (3 hrs)”. A receipt that works as a ticket: Booking, vehicle and payment details, the price broken into rate, service charge and tax, and the QR code to scan at the parking spot. Phone and OTP to start: Sign-in is a phone number and a one-time code, with an illustration that says what the app does: find parking near you by tapping a button. One system on app, web and for vendors: The website mirrors the map and receipt for planning ahead, and a vendor app serves the attendants at the lots.

What MyParkings does: Live availability: Capacity, occupied and free slots for each lot. Advance booking: Book by date, time and hours, for a car or a bike. QR check-in and out: Scan at the gate; no paper slip. Wallet and cashless pay: A closed wallet for payments, refunds and cashback. Passes and favourites: Regular commuters save lots and buy passes. Vendor app: Attendants manage check-ins at the lot. Outcome: MyParkings launched publicly in October 2021 for the South Delhi Municipal Corporation, with integration with FASTag, Vahan and e-challan planned. It passed 25,000 downloads across platforms, 10K+ of them on Google Play. Honest limits: Prices and names in the screens are sample data; the app is operated by the corporation’s partners, so usage data is theirs.

GrinHits (Grocery Delivery). Grinhits is a quick-commerce grocery service for Noida and Ghaziabad, fresh vegetables first, then milk, dairy, bakery and meat, delivered to the door in less than a day. Think Zepto, for a local market. I led the design of the brand, the app and the website. Service: Fresh vegetables, milk, dairy, bakery, groceries and meat, delivered daily Area: Noida and Ghaziabad at launch, with more cities planned Users: Families ordering the week’s food on phone or web Platforms: iOS, Android and the web The problem: Daily essentials in Indian cities were moving online fast, and big apps were racing to deliver in minutes. Grinhits set out to win its own neighbourhood: fresh produce from farms, sensible prices set for the local area, and delivery free above a basket size. To compete with the giants it had to feel just as quick and trustworthy. How do you make a new local grocer feel as fast and reliable as the national apps, and get people to fill a basket big enough to make delivery pay?

Price depends on place: Rates are set for Noida and Ghaziabad, so the app has to know where you are before it shows a price. A visible goal grows the basket: Showing how much more is needed for free delivery nudges people to add one more item. Freshness is shown, not told: Large, clean product photos sell vegetables better than any badge. Goals: Order in a minute: Search, categories and quick add from home. Bigger baskets: Order minimums and free delivery made visible and motivating. Trust after checkout: A clear bill, payment status and live order tracking.

Key decisions: Location first: The delivery address sits at the top of home, and product pages ask where you are, with a zip code or Detect, because prices are shown for Noida and Ghaziabad. A cart with a progress bar: The floating cart shows items, total and the delivery slot, above two goals: the amount still needed to place the order, and the amount for free delivery. Quick add everywhere: Product cards carry weight, price, MRP struck through and a plus button, so most things go in the basket without opening them. Order details as reassurance: Order number and date, cancel and FAQs at hand, the delivery address, the bill with discount and delivery charges, payment confirmed by UPI, a receipt to download, and a status line from ordered to delivered. Phone sign-in, or skip it: Name and phone with an OTP, social sign-in, a line on why the number is safe, and Skip login to browse first. A fresh, leafy brand: A wordmark with a leaf in the G, deep green for the brand, a bright green for every action, and warm category colours for offers. The web as a shop window: Free delivery in under 24 hours up front, offers by category, and how it works in three steps: order online, fresh farmed vegetables, doorstep delivery.

What Grinhits does: Categories and search: Vegetables, dairy, bakery, non-veg and groceries, with voice search. Offers: Category deals and banners on home. Smart cart: Order minimum, free-delivery goal and delivery slot. Area pricing: Prices set by location, checked by zip code. Order tracking: Status from ordered to packed, shipped and delivered. UPI and receipts: Payment confirmation and a downloadable receipt. Outcome: Grinhits launched in Noida and Ghaziabad with the app and website designed together, one brand and one basket across both. Honest limits: A small local start-up with little public record; the story is read from the delivered screens, names in them are blurred, and some onboarding copy is placeholder text from the design stage.

Fundoo-Learning (Quiz Game). Fundoo Learning began as Knowledge Box, an old quiz app with a weak interface and accessibility problems. The brief was a complete redesign plus new features: more quiz options, competing with others and hints. I led it with design thinking and turned the quizzes into a game: pick a subject, beat the clock, earn reward points and climb a global leaderboard. Its line: unlocking knowledge at the speed of thought. Product: A subject quiz game with reward points and leaderboards Before: Knowledge Box, an older quiz app, redesigned end to end Process: Design thinking: empathise, define, ideate, prototype, test Released: Google Play, October 2021 The problem: Knowledge Box entertained people with quizzes, but its interface was poorly designed and had several UX and accessibility issues. The stakeholders wanted a complete change of design and new features: multiple quiz options, competing with others and hints. Because a quiz game has no single user base, I chose inclusive design, designing for one so that it works for many.

A stakeholder workshop to gather the requirements, then a survey offline and online with three simple questions: which topics people like most in a quiz, how they want a quiz game on mobile to feel, and the pros and cons of the quiz game they play now. Sketches came out of stakeholder interviews and internal brainstorming, then wireframes before any visual design. How do you redesign something boring into a whole new level of interactivity and fun, for people who play quizzes to relax as much as to learn? Winning should be worth something: Allen, a product designer who plays to stay sharp, is the only competitor he can compare himself with, and nothing rewards a win. Low interactivity bores people: Stella, an account manager who plays to unwind, loses interest in static games and gets demotivated when she loses without knowing the answer. Keep it minimal: Both want something simple: a clear question, a clear result.

Goals: Clean and interactive: A simple, accessible interface with strong contrast. Gamification: Rewards, rankings and quick feedback to keep people playing. Smarter questions: AI-powered question suggestions matched to the player.

Key decisions: Subjects as cards with progress: Home asks “What do you want to improve?” and shows each subject as an illustrated card with a play button and how much of it you have completed. A quiz with a clock and help: Question count, a progress bar and a countdown timer above one question at a time, with hints to use when stuck and an explanation after. Feedback that motivates: Right or wrong comes with a short quote to encourage the player, and results show wrong in coral, right in green and skipped in amber, with the time taken. Points worth claiming: Reward points appear in large gold with a crown coin and Claim Rewards the moment a quiz ends; points are redeemed with email confirmation. A leaderboard with you in it: Your rank, points and score are pinned in violet above the global top three, so the gap is always visible. Accessible by colour: White backgrounds with dark text for contrast and readability, and colour modification for accessibility throughout. A playful brand: A wordmark whose double o is a pair of glasses, violet and blue, and bright 3D-style subject icons.

What Fundoo does: Subject quizzes: Physics, general knowledge, history, mathematics and more. Timed questions with hints: A countdown, progress and help on every quiz. Results breakdown: Right, wrong, skipped and time, then the full summary. Reward points: Earned per quiz, claimed and redeemed in the app. Leaderboards: My ranking and the global ranking. Invite friends: Bring others in to play and compete. Outcome: Fundoo Learning was released on Google Play in October 2021 as a free education app, built on this design; the full process is in the case study linked above. Honest limits: A short-lived product with no public usage data; names in the screens are sample data and some onboarding copy is placeholder text.

CityPark (Parking). Citipark is a parking app for busy cities: find a safe parking spot that suits you, see the facilities before you go, book ahead, pay cashless, navigate to the lot and extend your time from your phone. I designed it end to end with the Double Diamond process, from interviews and competitor analysis to personas, journeys, information architecture, wireframes, the brand and the final app. Audience: Drivers aged 18 to 60 in metro cities, all genders Core task: Search, book and pay for parking nearby, then navigate to it Platforms: Mobile, tablet and web Process: Double Diamond: research, define, ideate, prototype, validate The problem: Finding a parking space can be painful. The parking apps people used lacked practicality and had a poor experience: no accurate spot that matched their needs, few cashless options, nothing about the facilities at a lot, no way to choose a slot or extend time, and maps that did not find parking.

I interviewed regular car users about how they park. Almost all of them take the car out every day, almost all expect a mobile app rather than an offline process, they face poor spots, cash-only lots and bad apps, and they prefer cashless. Few compare parking rates, but they were willing to try. A competitor analysis of My Parkings, Parking Rhino and Get My Parking showed that none offered navigation to the lot or told people about the other services there, and one had no reservation history. Citipark set out to cover all seven: digital payments, slot reservation, history, navigation, price comparison, live availability and other services. How do you take the guesswork out of parking, from where to go to how to pay and when to leave? Certainty first: Nikhil, a sales manager in Noida who drives to client meetings all day, wants a cashless way to book a spot before he arrives; queues and full lots make him late. Plan, then go: Shruti, a homemaker in New Delhi who shops and meets friends, wants to know about availability and pricing in advance and an easy way to navigate there.

The pain peaks at the gate: The journey map dips at payment, finding a spot in the lot and finding the car again: the app has to help there, not just at booking. Goals: Find the right spot: Safe, suitable parking by vehicle, price and facilities. Book and pay in a few taps: Advance booking, cashless options, clear costs. Stay in control: Navigation, check-in by QR, extend time with an alert before it runs out.

Key decisions: A map with prices on the pins: Home is the map, filtered by car or bike, each lot a pin with its hourly rate, and quick filters for parking, open now and car wash. Facilities before you book: Each lot shows photos, rating, hours, spots available and the starting price, then amenities such as rooftop, EV charging, disabled spots and security. Reserve with dates and times: Start and end date and time in one sheet, then a choice of credit or debit card, Apple Pay or Google Pay. Activities with a live clock: Active, upcoming and history tabs; an active booking shows a countdown, Extend time and Check out, and overtime is shown with what it will cost. Check in by QR, cancel with clarity: A QR code to scan at the lot, and a cancel dialog that states the refund before you confirm. Your vehicles, fetched for you: Choose car or bike and enter the registration number; the app builds the car profile and keeps a list of vehicles to manage. Help and recent searches at hand: Search opens on recent places and a help card with FAQs and contact, and booking details close with why to use Citipark: offers, car services and 24/7 support.

What Citipark does: Map search: Lots with live prices, filtered by vehicle and service. Lot details: Photos, rating, hours, availability and amenities. Reservation: Date and time ranges, with card, Apple Pay or Google Pay. Activities: Active, upcoming and history, with extend and check-out. QR check-in: Scan at the lot; cancel with a stated refund. Vehicles and payments: Manage cars and bikes, cards and saved places. From research to screens: Empathy maps and pains and gains for both personas, then a user journey map across finding a lot, asking about availability, taking a ticket, paying, finding a spot, finding the exit and finding the car. A user flow from splash, onboarding, login and OTP to adding a vehicle, then four tabs: home, activities, saved and more; and an information architecture built by card sorting. Paper sketches, then low-fidelity wireframes to avoid late changes and explain the design to stakeholders, then the style guide and the final screens.

Outcome: A complete, research-led design for the whole parking journey, documented step by step in the case study linked above. Honest limits: A design case study; names, cards and numbers in the screens are sample data.

Jobbers (Job Search). Jobbers is a job-finder app and website. Finding a job is hard enough; finding one that matches your profile is harder, and a competitive analysis showed most job portals had weak interfaces and flows that were hard to follow. I led the design of a fresh, colourful app for iOS and Android and a web layout, built around a professional profile, simple search and gamification that keeps people engaged. Platforms: iOS, Android and the web Deliverables: UI, UX and interactions Duration: 3 months Approach: Rethink, redesign, increase The problem: Job portals are where careers start, yet most of them were cluttered and confusing. The challenge was to update the whole interface with current design trends while keeping the brand’s identity, make every journey as easy as possible, and show each person the most relevant information. Research and strategy came in three parts: data analysis of the product’s usage and trends, a competitive analysis of competitors and market leaders, and focus groups and interviews, watching real users to reduce confusion.

We rethought the product by analysing it and its flows for pain points, redesigned it in a new style that solved them, and increased its reach with an iOS and Android app and a web layout tailored to their users. How do you make looking for a job feel hopeful instead of hopeless? Profiles do the selling: Recruiters respond to a complete, professional profile, so completing it should feel like progress. Relevance beats volume: People want the jobs that fit them first, by category, not an endless list. Engagement needs a reason: Stats, matches and a sense of momentum keep a job search going. Goals: Professional profile: A strong profile, shareable with recruiters in a tap. Search that fits: Categories, filters and the most relevant jobs first. Apply or save: Apply from the job page or keep it in favourites.

Key decisions: Easy, fast account creation: Sign-up asks only for the essentials, then you choose your category (UX/UI designer, frontend developer, brand designer and more) and land on a home tailored to it. A home of personalised offers: “Are you ready to join your dream job?” with search, categories, popular jobs from known companies and a post-a-job tab for employers. A profile that shows momentum: Applied, reviewed and match percentage, recruiters who viewed your résumé, and a Complete your profile bar with Update CV. Skills you can adjust: Skills such as Figma and Adobe XD as sliders, so your level is clear to recruiters. Messages with rich media: Chat with recruiters, sharing documents, photos, music, video and contacts in the thread. Help in one place: A help centre with chat, FAQs and email support. Colour with a purpose: Blue as the colour of trust, violet and mint for energy, wavy edges and a ribbon logo; gamification in the colours keeps people interacting longer.

What Jobbers does: Professional profile: Share your details with recruiters in a tap. Job search: Search, categories and in-app filters. Apply or save: Apply from the job page or save to favourites. Messages: Chat with recruiters and share files. Skills and CV: Adjust skills and keep your CV current. Website: A web layout to find jobs and sign up. From flow to screens: A user flow from home to search, a list of opportunities and the vacancy page, then applying, documents, questions from the employer, revise and submit. Wireframes for the concept and journey testing, then the visual design: fresh, clean and minimal, content first, with catchy colours. Outcome: A complete app and website concept for job seekers and employers, documented in the case study linked above. Honest limits: A design concept; company names and logos in the screens illustrate the kind of employers listed, and names and numbers are sample data.

AstroBaba (Astrology Consulting). Astro Baba is an online marketplace of verified astrologers in India: chat, call or video-call an astrologer, with the first three minutes free, and read daily horoscopes, your kundli, tarot, numerology and love match in between. I designed the app, from the onboarding and the astrologer profiles to the wallet, the horoscope and the compatibility tools. Product: Consultations with verified astrologers by chat, call or video Topics: Love, health, career, finance, marriage and education Languages: More than eight Indian languages Releases: Version 1.3 in December 2020 to 4.1 in September 2021 The problem: People across India consult astrologers for the big decisions: marriage, a career move, money, health. Finding a trustworthy one usually means word of mouth and a visit. Astro Baba put verified astrologers a tap away and paid them by the minute, so the design had to build trust in a stranger and make paying per minute feel fair. How do you help someone choose an astrologer they have never met, and make a per-minute consultation feel safe to start?

Trust is in the profile: Experience, languages, followers, people served and ratings decide who gets the call. A free start lowers the stakes: The first minutes free and a ₹1 offer get people to try. Daily reasons to return: Horoscopes, check-ins and love match bring people back between consultations. Goals: Choose with confidence: Rich astrologer profiles with expertise and availability. Pay simply: A wallet with fast recharge, coupons and coins. Come back daily: Free tools around the paid consultation.

Key decisions: Profiles that answer “why this one”: Photo, rating, city, verified badge, years of experience and languages; followers and people served; expertise (health, marriage, finance, education) and skills (Vedic, psychic reading, anushthanam); the price per minute, the free minutes and whether they are online or busy. Chat or call, or book a slot: Two large buttons for chat and call, and the astrologer’s weekly availability with Book Now. A wallet that nudges, gently: Astro wallet and coins at the top, a low-balance warning, fast-recharge amounts, a ₹1 for 10 free minutes offer, coupons and payment by Paytm or card. A hub of free tools: Daily horoscope, kundli, tarot, love meter, numerology, panchang, palmistry and match making as icons on the profile, with a daily check-in streak and coins. The horoscope as a dashboard: Yesterday, today and tomorrow; physical, emotional and intellectual scores as rings; do’s and don’ts, lucky numbers and colours, then recommended astrologers. Love match in two taps: Choose two zodiac signs, calculate, and see an overall percentage with a reading and astrologers to consult. A door for astrologers: Sign-in with Apple, Google or Facebook for users, and “I am astrologer” for the people on the other side.

What Astro Baba does: Consultations: Chat, voice and private video calls with astrologers. Live sessions: Ask questions during astrologers’ live streams. Daily horoscope: For all twelve signs, with scores and advice. Kundli and more: Kundli, tarot, numerology, panchang and palmistry. Love match: Compatibility between two signs. Wallet and coins: Recharge, coupons, rewards and referrals. Outcome: Astro Baba launched on Android and iOS and grew through releases from version 1.3 in December 2020 to 4.1 in September 2021, adding live chat, the free first three minutes and reward coins. Honest limits: Agency work; usage data stayed with the client. Some copy in the screens is placeholder text from the design stage.

AppInfinity Solutions (Company Website). AppInfinity Solutions is an outsourcing company that runs inbound and outbound calls and IT staffing for clients around the world, with a team working around the clock. I led the design of its website: a brand-led home and about page that explain the services and make it easy to get in touch. Client: AppInfinity Solutions Services: Inbound calls, outbound calls, IT staffing Audience: Companies looking to outsource customer support and staffing Scope: Home and about pages, in the brand’s infinity identity The problem: Outsourcing is sold on trust: a client hands its customers or its hiring to someone else. The old presence did not show the people, the scale or the round-the-clock service behind the company. The website had to make a small firm look established and make contact effortless. How do you make an outsourcing firm feel like a safe pair of hands from the first screen? People sell support: Faces with headsets and a real office say more than any claim.

Contact must always be one tap away: Email, phone and 24x7 hours belong at the top of every page. Proof up front: Reviews, client counts and technology partners reassure before anyone reads further. Goals: Explain the services: Inbound, outbound and IT staffing, clearly separated. Build trust: People, proof and partners on the first screen. Start conversations: Contact Us and call-back everywhere. Key decisions: Contact in the top bar: Email, phone number and 24x7 working hours sit above the navigation on every page, with a Contact Us button. Proof in the hero: “Embrace digital for a better future” with client reviews, a client count, a review card and technology partners beside a support agent. The logo as a window: The about page frames the real office inside the infinity mark: the brand and the team in one image. A friendly welcome: “Welcome to App Infinity” with an agent at work, a chat bubble offering help, and a call-back button. Services by what clients need: Navigation by inbound, outbound, IT staffing and services, so each client finds their line of work at once.

What the site covers: Home: Hero, proof, welcome and services. About: Mission, team and the infinity identity. Inbound and outbound: Call-centre services for clients. IT staffing: Staff for clients’ technology teams. Contact: Top bar, Contact Us and call-back. Partners: Technology partners and client reviews. Outcome: The site gave AppInfinity a consistent brand and a clear way for prospective clients to understand its services and get in touch. Honest limits: Placeholder copy and sample reviews from the design stage remain in the screens; no traffic data is claimed.

Yaye (Yoga & Wellness Booking). Yaye is a yoga and wellness booking app: discover yoga studios, ashrams, wellness retreats, Ayurvedic spas and cruises near you, compare them, and book a stay or a session with the day’s deals. I designed the app and its lotus brand. Product: Booking for yoga studios, ashrams, retreats and spas Users: People looking for yoga and wellness, and the vendors who host them Platform: Mobile app Brand: A lotus mark and a bold wordmark on deep violet The problem: Yoga and wellness options are scattered: studios on maps, ashrams by word of mouth, retreats on travel sites. Yaye brings them together so people can find, compare and book in one place, and gives studios and ashrams a channel of their own. How do you make booking a retreat or a yoga studio feel calm, the way the experience itself should feel? Browse by kind: People start from what they want, yoga, an ashram, a spa, not from a place name. Photos decide: Studios and ashrams sell on how they look and what is around them. Two sides: Vendors need their own way in to list and manage their places.

Goals: Discover easily: Categories, nearby studios and top ashrams on home. Decide with confidence: Amenities, gallery, ratings and things nearby. Book in a few steps: Dates, guests, deals and a clear total. Key decisions: Categories as photo circles: Ayurvedic spa, wellness cruise, wellness retreat, ashrams, yoga studios, spiritual retreat, yoga and health resorts, each with a photo. Places that show themselves: A studio page opens on photos, open-now status and its story, then amenities, things to do nearby, a gallery and reviews. Deals with a deadline: Daily steal deals with a countdown, discount badges and an offers page, so a booking feels well timed. A clear review before paying: Dates, guests, traveller details, GST, the grand total, promo codes and Pay now on one screen. User or vendor: Choosing a role at the start gives studios and ashrams their own path. A calm, confident brand: A lotus mark, deep violet with a lighter violet for actions, and friendly meditative illustration.

What Yaye does: Discover: Categories, studios nearby and top ashrams. Place pages: Amenities, gallery, nearby and reviews. Offers: Daily deals and promo codes. Booking: Dates, guests and payment. My trips and favourites: Booked and saved places. Vendors: A separate role for studios and ashrams. Outcome: A complete app design for discovering and booking yoga and wellness, with its own brand. Honest limits: A design project; names and prices in the screens are sample data and some copy is placeholder text. A phone number in the screens is blurred.

Alpha Match (Marketplace). Alpha Match is a Toronto pet marketplace: one place to find a pet locally or abroad, and to post and promote pets, pet services, products and events. It serves pet owners, buyers and breeders, from dogs and cats to birds, fish, reptiles and horses. I designed the mobile app’s journeys for each of those people and the Figma component library it was built from. Client: Alpha Match Inc, Toronto Users: Pet buyers and owners, breeders, and pet businesses Platforms: iOS and Android Delivered: Multi-persona journeys and a Figma component library The problem: Finding a pet, a groomer or a breeder usually means classifieds, social groups and word of mouth, and pet businesses have few places built for them to reach owners. Alpha Match wanted all of it in one app: listings for pets, services, products and events, with the people behind them a message away. How do you design one app that works for someone looking for a puppy, a breeder listing a litter and a shop promoting its services, without any of them feeling it was made for someone else?

Many personas, one feed: Buyers browse, breeders and businesses post; the same listing card has to serve both sides. Posting is the business: Listings, featured placement and memberships pay for the platform, so adding a listing has to be one tap from anywhere. Pets are emotional: The tone should be warm and playful, never like a classifieds site. Goals: Find fast: Search, categories and filters for type, location and price. Post easily: A listing in a few steps, with photos and video. Build once: A component library so every screen stays consistent.

Key decisions: A plus at the centre: A raised yellow plus button sits in the middle of the tab bar, so creating a listing is always one tap away, for every persona. One listing card for everything: Photo or video, title, location, price and a type tag: the same card carries a pet, a service, a product or an event. Bold brand, calm screens: The crest’s gold becomes a bright yellow for actions and headers on black, while the content screens stay white so photos of the animals lead. Illustrated moments: Permission prompts, confirmations and success states get a friendly illustration and one clear button, instead of a system alert. A library, not a set of screens: Cards, buttons, tabs, inputs and dialogs were built as Figma components with variants, so new journeys were assembled rather than redrawn.

What the app does: Listings feed: Pets, services, products and events, with photos and video. Search and filters: Categories, location, listing type and price range. Post a listing: From the plus button, with featured placement for more reach. Messaging and favourites: Contact the lister in the app and save listings for later. Accounts: Sign up with email, Facebook or Apple; connections, settings and upgrades. Memberships: Monthly and annual plans for people and businesses who post often. Outcome: Alpha Match launched on the App Store and Google Play under the line “Everything pets.”, with a consistent app assembled from the component library. Honest limits: Few public details survive; the journeys and decisions here are read from the delivered screens, and usage data stayed with the client.
